```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
set.seed(2026) # bootstrap intervals reproducible across builds
for (pkg in c("tidyverse", "kableExtra", "patchwork")) {
  suppressMessages(
    library(pkg, character.only = TRUE, quietly = TRUE)
  )
}
```

GMITS extends the classical grey-system GM(1,1) model to irregularly
spaced reporting intervals, aimed at early-stage outbreak forecasting
when only a handful of data points are available. This page collects
the shared methodology, checks it on synthetic data, and evaluates it on
real-time snapshots of the 2022 England mpox outbreak, forecasting from
the first n weekly reports (n = 4–8) as the outbreak unfolded. Earlier
applications to two food-borne outbreaks are on the
[Bongkrekic Acid Food Poisoning (2024)](Bongkrekic_Acid_2024.html) and
[2011 Listeria Outbreak](Listeria_2011.html) pages.

## Functions {-}

All pages load the same function file, `R/gmits_functions.R`.
The regression in `gmits()` was corrected on 2026-10-13; see the
[revision history](#revision-history).

```{r functions, file = "R/gmits_functions.R"}
```

---

# Synthetic Validation

Validates that GMITS recovers known parameters from noise-free,
irregularly spaced data. A 2 × 2 design crosses direction (growth,
a < 0; decay, a > 0) with speed (|a| = 0.3 or 0.4 per day), holding
b, the first value and the time grid fixed, so that the effects of
direction and speed can be read separately. The same four series are
also fitted on an equally spaced grid with the same mean interval.

```{r synth-validate}
# Generate x0 from the ODE solution with known (a, b, x0[1])
synth_series <- function(a, b, x0_1, t_pts) {
  x1 <- (x0_1 - b / a) * exp(-a * t_pts) + b / a
  c(x0_1, diff(x1) / diff(t_pts))
}

t_irr     <- c(0, 2, 4, 7, 10)   # irregular gaps: 2, 2, 3, 3
t_eq      <- seq(0, 10, by = 2.5) # equal gaps, same mean interval
n_ahead_s <- 3
b_s       <- 5
x0_1_s    <- 8

# 2 x 2 design: direction (growth / decay) x speed (|a| = 0.3 / 0.4),
# with b, x0[1] and the time grid held fixed
synth_scen <- expand_grid(
  direction = c("Growth", "Decay"),
  abs_a = c(0.3, 0.4)
) |>
  mutate(a = if_else(direction == "Growth", -abs_a, abs_a))

fit_synth <- function(a, t_fit) {
  dt_mean <- mean(diff(t_fit))
  t_all <- c(t_fit, max(t_fit) + dt_mean * seq_len(n_ahead_s))
  x0 <- synth_series(a, b_s, x0_1_s, t_fit)
  r <- gmits(x0, as.Date("2024-01-01") + t_fit, n_ahead = n_ahead_s)
  list(
    a_hat = r$a,
    traj = tibble(
      t = t_all,
      True = synth_series(a, b_s, x0_1_s, t_all),
      Fitted = c(r$x0_hat, r$x0_future),
      Forecast = rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), c(length(t_fit), n_ahead_s))
    )
  )
}

synth_res <- synth_scen |>
  mutate(
    irr = map(a, fit_synth, t_fit = t_irr),
    eq = map(a, fit_synth, t_fit = t_eq),
    a_hat = map_dbl(irr, "a_hat"),
    shrink_irr = a_hat / a,
    shrink_eq = map_dbl(eq, "a_hat") / a,
    # exact attenuation for an exponential on an equal grid
    shrink_theory = 1 / ((abs_a * 2.5 / 2) / tanh(abs_a * 2.5 / 2)),
    fc_err_3 = map_dbl(irr, function(f) {
      x <- tail(f$traj, 1)
      100 * (x$Fitted - x$True) / x$True
    })
  )

synth_res |>
  select(direction, a, a_hat, shrink_irr, shrink_eq, shrink_theory,
         fc_err_3) |>
  kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Direction", "True a", "GMITS a (irregular grid)",
      "a_hat / a, irregular grid", "a_hat / a, equal grid",
      "Theory, equal grid", "Forecast error at step 3 (%)"
    ),
    caption = paste0(
      "GMITS parameter recovery on noise-free synthetic data ",
      "(b = 5, x0[1] = 8)"
    )
  ) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```

```{r plot-synth-validate, fig.height = 8.5}
df_synth <- synth_res |>
  select(direction, abs_a, irr) |>
  mutate(traj = map(irr, "traj")) |>
  select(-irr) |>
  unnest(traj) |>
  mutate(
    rel_err = 100 * (Fitted - True) / True,
    direction = factor(direction, levels = c("Growth", "Decay")),
    speed = factor(paste0("|a| = ", abs_a))
  )

# Repeat the last fitted point in the forecast segment so the dashed
# forecast line starts where the solid fitted line ends
df_synth_plot <- bind_rows(
  df_synth |> filter(!Forecast) |> mutate(segment = "in-sample"),
  df_synth |>
    filter(Forecast | t == max(t_irr)) |>
    mutate(segment = "forecast")
) |>
  pivot_longer(c(True, Fitted), names_to = "type", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = c("in-sample", "forecast")))

synth_boundary <- geom_vline(
  xintercept = max(t_irr) + mean(diff(t_irr)) / 2,
  linetype = "dotted", color = "grey60"
)
synth_x <- expression("Time (days from " * t[0] * ")")
synth_xscale <- scale_x_continuous(limits = range(df_synth$t))
speed_cols <- c("|a| = 0.3" = "#86b6ef", "|a| = 0.4" = "#1c5cab")

p_values <- ggplot(
  df_synth_plot,
  aes(t, value, color = type, linetype = segment,
      group = interaction(type, segment))
) +
  synth_boundary +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = df_synth_plot |> filter(segment == "in-sample", type == "True"),
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(True = "black", Fitted = "steelblue"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("in-sample" = "solid", "forecast" = "dashed"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  # one row per speed, one column per direction; each panel its own y
  facet_wrap(
    ~ speed + direction, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y",
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(multi_line = FALSE)
  ) +
  synth_xscale +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Period incidence")

p_error <- ggplot(
  df_synth |> filter(t > 0),
  aes(t, rel_err, color = speed)
) +
  synth_boundary +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = Forecast), size = 2.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = speed_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = 16, "TRUE" = 1),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "in-sample", "TRUE" = "forecast"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  # free_y keeps both panels' axes drawn (so they line up with the top
  # rows); the fixed limits keep one common scale
  facet_wrap(~ direction, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = range(c(0, df_synth$rel_err))) +
  synth_xscale +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = synth_x, y = "Relative error (%)")

p_values / p_error +
  plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "GMITS Synthetic Validation — Parameter Recovery",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Top: black = true ODE, blue = GMITS fit + 3-step forecast ",
      "(b = 5, x0[1] = 8, irregular grid).\n",
      "Bottom: (GMITS - true) / true, same y scale in both panels. ",
      "Dotted line = forecast boundary."
    )
  )
```

**Implementation note.** An earlier version of this page attributed
a much larger growth-phase underprediction to the background value;
most of it was an implementation error, corrected on 2026-10-13
([revision history](#revision-history)). With the corrected regression GMITS
recovers every $a$ in the table to within
`r round(100 * max(abs(1 - synth_res$shrink_irr)), 1)`%.

**Remaining limitation — background-value bias.**
The residual gaps are the approximation bias of the GM(1,1) family. The
background value $z_{k} = \frac{1}{2}(x^{(1)}_{k} + x^{(1)}_{k-1})$
replaces the interval mean of $x^{(1)}$ by the mean of its endpoints.
When $x^{(1)}$ is curved this misstates the interval mean: in a growth
phase $x^{(1)}$ is convex and the endpoint mean *overstates* it; in a
decay phase $x^{(1)}$ is concave and the endpoint mean *understates* it.
In both cases the error is proportional to the distance of $x^{(1)}$
from its asymptote $b/a$, so the regression slope is attenuated and
$|\hat a|$ is pulled towards zero by the factor
$1 / [(h/2)\coth(h/2)]$ with $h = |a|\,\Delta t$, whatever the sign of
$a$: about 8% at $h = 1$ and under 0.1% at $h = 0.1$. Only the sign of
the resulting forecast error differs: a growth forecast grows too slowly
(underprediction) and a decay forecast decays too slowly
(overprediction).

The 2 × 2 design separates the three influences on this bias:

- **Speed:** a larger $|a|$ shrinks $|\hat a|$ more in both directions
  (equal grid: `r sprintf("%.3f", synth_res$shrink_eq[synth_res$a == 0.3])`
  at $|a| = 0.3$ vs.
  `r sprintf("%.3f", synth_res$shrink_eq[synth_res$a == 0.4])` at
  $|a| = 0.4$), and the forecast error grows with the horizon.
- **Direction:** on the equally spaced grid growth and decay are shrunk by
  exactly the same factor, which matches the theoretical value, so the
  direction of the trend on its own does not matter.
- **Spacing:** on the irregular grid (intervals 2, 2, 3, 3 days) growth is
  shrunk more than decay
  (`r sprintf("%.3f", synth_res$shrink_irr[synth_res$a == -0.3])` vs.
  `r sprintf("%.3f", synth_res$shrink_irr[synth_res$a == 0.3])` at
  $|a| = 0.3$). A growing $x^{(1)}$ changes most over the long late
  intervals, where the trapezoid error is largest, whereas a decaying
  $x^{(1)}$ changes most over the short early ones. Uneven reporting
  intervals therefore matter more when an outbreak is accelerating.

On a linear axis the decay fits look almost perfect only because the
counts approach zero; the relative-error panel shows the forecasts
drifting upwards by up to
`r round(max(synth_res$fc_err_3))`% after three steps.

This limitation is well-known in the grey system literature (Liu, 2025;
Liu & Deng, 2000) and is the motivation for optimising the background
coefficient $\alpha$ (replacing the fixed 0.5). That extension is outside
the scope of this study; the bias is reported here as an explicit boundary
condition for GMITS applicability: **the method is most reliable when
$|a| \times \overline{\Delta t}$ is small**, i.e., moderate growth rates
and short reporting intervals.

# Data: 2022 England mpox outbreak

Mpox spread from person to person, so early incidence grows roughly
exponentially and the GMITS growth coefficient can be read as a growth
rate. (The two food-borne outbreaks analysed earlier are common-source
events whose epicurves are shaped by exposure timing and the incubation
period, not by transmission; they are kept as supplementary examples on
the [Bongkrekic acid](Bongkrekic_Acid_2024.html) and
[Listeria](Listeria_2011.html) pages.)

The data come from the repository accompanying Overton et al. (2023),
*Nowcasting the 2022 mpox outbreak in England* (arXiv:2302.09076),
released under CC0. Three parts are used:

- **Ground truth:** daily cases by specimen date after all backfilling.
- **Real-time snapshots:** the reporting triangle as it stood on day
  *T*, i.e. only the cases that had been reported by then.
- **Reporting-delay distribution:** the Weibull parameters the authors
  estimated from individual-level data with a right-truncation
  correction, supplied with each snapshot (one set for ordinary days and
  one for days affected by weekend processing).

Dates are anonymised in the source, so the x-axis is a day index.
Symptom-onset snapshots start after the peak, so the specimen-date series
is used. Daily counts drop sharply at weekends, so counts are summed into
non-overlapping 7-day weeks ending on the snapshot day.

```{r data-mpox}
mpox_dir <- "data/mpox_england"
snapshots <- seq(75, 100, by = 5)

truth_daily <- read_csv(
  file.path(mpox_dir, "full_data_specimen.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Daily counts reported by day T, plus the probability that a case from
# that day had been reported by T. For specimen dates the authors model
# the cell probability for delay index dev as W(dev - 1) - W(dev - 2),
# where W is the Weibull CDF; dev = T - origin + 1 is the latest observed
# cell, so P(reported by T) = W(T - origin).
snapshot_daily <- function(t_snap) {
  read_csv(
    file.path(
      mpox_dir,
      paste0("nowcasting_input_specimen_", t_snap, ".csv")
    ),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
    group_by(origin) |>
    summarise(
      n = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      shape = first(var1),
      scale = first(var2),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(p_report = pweibull(t_snap - origin, shape, scale))
}

week_sum <- function(daily, week_ends) {
  sapply(week_ends, function(e) {
    sum(daily$n[daily$origin > e - 7 & daily$origin <= e])
  })
}

# Nowcast-adjusted weekly totals: inflate days with P(reported) >= 0.5;
# days below that are treated as missing and filled with the mean of the
# adjusted days in the same week.
week_nowcast <- function(daily, week_ends, p_min = 0.5) {
  daily <- daily |>
    mutate(adj = nowcast_inflate(n, p_report, p_min))
  sapply(week_ends, function(e) {
    adj <- daily$adj[daily$origin > e - 7 & daily$origin <= e]
    mean(adj, na.rm = TRUE) * 7
  })
}
```

The adjustment uses only what was known on day *T*: the reported counts
and the delay distribution estimated at that time. The 0.5 threshold
(inflation factor at most 2) was fixed before looking at the outcomes.

```{r plot-mpox-epicurve, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(truth_daily |> filter(origin <= 160), aes(origin, n)) +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = min(snapshots) - 0.5, xmax = max(snapshots) + 0.5,
    ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.08
  ) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60", width = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = snapshots, linetype = "dotted", color = "#2a78d6"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "England mpox 2022 — daily cases by specimen date",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Backfilled ground truth; dotted lines = forecast origins ",
      "(snapshots T = 75, 80, ..., 100)"
    ),
    x = "Day index (anonymised)", y = "Cases"
  )
```

How incomplete were the most recent data at each snapshot, and how much
does the nowcast recover?

```{r mpox-completeness}
completeness <- tibble(snapshot = snapshots) |>
  mutate(
    reported = map_dbl(snapshot, function(t) {
      week_sum(snapshot_daily(t), t)
    }),
    nowcast = map_dbl(snapshot, function(t) {
      week_nowcast(snapshot_daily(t), t)
    }),
    final = map_dbl(snapshot, function(t) week_sum(truth_daily, t)),
    pct = 100 * reported / final,
    pct_nowcast = 100 * nowcast / final
  )

completeness |>
  select(snapshot, reported, nowcast, final, pct, pct_nowcast) |>
  kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c(
      "Snapshot T", "Last week, reported", "Last week, nowcast",
      "Last week, final", "Reported (% of final)",
      "Nowcast (% of final)"
    ),
    caption = "Right truncation in the most recent week"
  ) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```

At the forecast origins only
`r round(min(completeness$pct))`–`r round(max(completeness$pct))`% of the
most recent week had been reported. The nowcast raises this to
`r round(min(completeness$pct_nowcast))`–`r round(max(completeness$pct_nowcast))`%:
it recovers part of the gap but still falls short, mainly because cases
from the last two to three days had barely been reported and reporting at
three to four days' delay was slower than the parametric delay
distribution implies.

# Forecasting from the First n Reports

This is the question GMITS was designed for: **when only the first n
weekly reports of an outbreak are available, how well do GMITS and the
exponential regression forecast, and how much do they improve as n
grows?**

Weeks are counted from the start of the outbreak. Week 1 covers days
48–54; the grid is fixed so that week 4 ends on day 75, the earliest
snapshot in the source data (a single case on day 46 falls before
week 1). After n weeks the forecast origin is T = 54 + 7(n − 1), so
n = 4, …, 8 corresponds to T = 75, 82, 89, 96 and 103. Each forecast uses
the snapshot of day T, so the latest week is right-truncated exactly as
it was in real time. Both models are fitted to the same inputs:

- **Reported:** counts as available on day *T* (right-truncated).
- **Nowcast:** the delay-based adjustment described above.
- **Oracle:** the backfilled counts for the same weeks, i.e. what a
  perfect truncation correction would give. Not available in real time;
  shown as a reference.
- **Reported ×1.5:** the most recent week scaled by a fixed factor; used
  only in the sliding-window comparison further below.

There is one forecast per n and horizon, so differences between
neighbouring values of n are single realisations from one outbreak
rather than averages.

```{r mpox-forecast-fns}
n_fit_m <- 5
n_ahead_m <- 2
input_levels <- c("Reported", "Reported ×1.5", "Nowcast", "Oracle")
model_cols <- c("GMITS" = "#2a78d6", "Exp. regression" = "#eb6834")

# Fit both models to every input version, using the n_fit weeks that end
# on the snapshot day, and forecast n_ahead_m weeks
run_snapshot <- function(t_snap, n_fit = n_fit_m) {
  fit_ends <- t_snap - 7 * rev(seq_len(n_fit) - 1)
  fut_ends <- t_snap + 7 * seq_len(n_ahead_m)
  fit_dates <- as.Date("2022-01-01") + fit_ends
  all_dates <- as.Date("2022-01-01") + c(fit_ends, fut_ends)

  daily <- snapshot_daily(t_snap)
  obs <- week_sum(daily, fit_ends)
  inputs <- list(
    "Reported" = obs,
    "Reported ×1.5" = truncation_adjust(obs, 1, 1.5),
    "Nowcast" = week_nowcast(daily, fit_ends),
    "Oracle" = week_sum(truth_daily, fit_ends)
  )

  imap_dfr(inputs, function(x, nm) {
    g <- gmits_boot(x, fit_dates, n_boot = 1000, n_ahead = n_ahead_m)
    # exp_reg() drops zero weeks, so rebuild fitted values on the full grid
    er <- exp_reg(x, fit_dates)
    t_all <- as.numeric(all_dates - er$date[1])
    bind_rows(
      tibble(
        model = "GMITS", point = g$point,
        lower = g$lower, upper = g$upper
      ),
      tibble(
        model = "Exp. regression",
        point = exp(er$alpha + er$beta * t_all),
        lower = NA_real_, upper = NA_real_
      )
    ) |>
      mutate(
        input_type = nm,
        input = rep(c(x, rep(NA, n_ahead_m)), 2),
        step = rep(seq_len(n_fit + n_ahead_m) - n_fit, 2),
        week_end = rep(c(fit_ends, fut_ends), 2),
        truth = rep(week_sum(truth_daily, c(fit_ends, fut_ends)), 2)
      )
  }) |>
    mutate(
      snapshot = t_snap,
      input_type = factor(input_type, levels = input_levels),
      model = factor(model, levels = names(model_cols))
    )
}
```

```{r first-n}
week1_end <- 54
n_grid <- 4:8

first_n_fc <- map_dfr(n_grid, function(n) {
  run_snapshot(week1_end + 7 * (n - 1), n_fit = n) |>
    mutate(n = n)
})

first_n_err <- first_n_fc |>
  filter(step > 0, input_type != "Reported ×1.5") |>
  mutate(
    ape = 100 * abs(point - truth) / truth,
    covered = truth >= lower & truth <= upper,
    horizon = factor(
      if_else(step == 1, "1 week ahead", "2 weeks ahead")
    ),
    input_type = droplevels(input_type)
  )
```

```{r plot-first-n-error, fig.height = 5.5}
ggplot(first_n_err, aes(n, ape, color = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_grid(horizon ~ input_type) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_grid) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast error from the first n weekly reports",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Absolute percentage error against final counts; ",
      "Oracle is not available in real time"
    ),
    x = "Number of weekly reports used (n)", y = "APE (%)"
  )
```

```{r first-n-table}
first_n_err |>
  filter(step == 1) |>
  select(n, snapshot, input_type, model, ape) |>
  mutate(col = paste(input_type, model, sep = ": ")) |>
  select(-input_type, -model) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = ape) |>
  left_join(
    first_n_err |>
      filter(step == 1, model == "GMITS", input_type == "Nowcast") |>
      select(n, covered),
    by = "n"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    covered = if_else(covered, "yes", "no"),
    last_week_pct = map_dbl(snapshot, function(t) {
      100 * week_sum(snapshot_daily(t), t) / week_sum(truth_daily, t)
    }),
    .after = snapshot
  ) |>
  kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c(
      "n", "Snapshot T", "Last week reported (%)",
      "GMITS", "Exp. reg.", "GMITS", "Exp. reg.", "GMITS", "Exp. reg.",
      "In GMITS 95% PI (nowcast)"
    ),
    caption = "One-week-ahead APE (%) from the first n weekly reports"
  ) |>
  add_header_above(c(
    " " = 3, "Reported" = 2, "Nowcast" = 2, "Oracle" = 2, " " = 1
  )) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```

```{r plot-first-n-forecast, fig.height = 6.5}
fn_plot <- first_n_fc |> filter(input_type == "Nowcast")
fn_truth <- first_n_fc |> distinct(n, week_end, truth, step)
fn_pts <- first_n_fc |>
  filter(
    model == "GMITS", step <= 0,
    input_type %in% c("Reported", "Nowcast")
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    data = fn_truth,
    aes(week_end, truth, alpha = step > 0),
    fill = "grey60", width = 5
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = fn_plot |> filter(step >= 0, !is.na(lower)),
    aes(week_end, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),

  geom_line(
    data = fn_plot,
    aes(week_end, point, color = model),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = fn_pts,
    aes(week_end, input, shape = input_type),
    size = 2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ n, labeller = label_both, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Reported" = 4, "Nowcast" = 16),
    labels = c("Reported" = "reported at T", "Nowcast" = "nowcast"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = 0.45, "TRUE" = 0.85),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "fit window (final)", "TRUE" = "forecast (final)"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, NA)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical") +
  labs(
    title = "Forecasts from the first n weekly reports (nowcast input)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Bars = final counts; crosses = reported at T; ",
      "dots = nowcast-adjusted\n",
      "Ribbon = GMITS 95% bootstrap PI (clipped at 0)"
    ),
    x = "Week ending (day index)", y = "Weekly cases"
  )
```

What the first-n forecasts show:

- **GMITS on the nowcast input improves quickly with n while growth is
  still exponential.** One week ahead its error falls from 61% (n = 4) to
  33%, 22% and 11% (n = 5–7); two weeks ahead from 70% to 30% and 5%
  (n = 4–6). At n = 8 (T = 103) the outbreak is close to its peak and the
  constant-rate extrapolation starts to overshoot (22% and 41%).
- **The exponential regression does not improve with n on corrected
  input; it gets worse** (one week ahead on the nowcast input: 50% at
  n = 4 to 181% at n = 8; on the oracle input 147–284% throughout).
  Because the window starts at the first week of the outbreak, the very
  small early counts dominate the log-linear slope, and the
  extrapolation overshoots further as growth slows.
- **On the raw reported input the regression looks excellent at n = 5–6
  (5% and 2%)**, but this is the same offsetting of errors seen in the
  sliding window: the truncated last week flattens a slope that would
  otherwise overshoot. It disappears once the input is corrected.
- **The GMITS intervals are not yet calibrated:** the final count fell
  inside the 95% interval in 2 of 5 one-week forecasts on the nowcast
  input.

One caveat limits what a single outbreak can show. Here n and the stage
of the outbreak move together: a larger n also means a forecast origin
closer to the peak, where any exponential extrapolation fails. Whether
GMITS's accuracy improves with n *at a fixed stage of growth* can only be
separated in the planned simulation study, where outbreaks with known
growth rates can be truncated at any n.

---

# Sliding Window: Last Five Weeks at Six Snapshots

As a complement, each of six snapshots (T = 75, 80, …, 100) uses only the
most recent 5 weeks (n = 5) rather than counting from the start of the
outbreak. Only the earliest snapshots coincide with the first reports;
the later ones ask how well a short recent window forecasts once the
outbreak is under way.

```{r forecast-mpox}
mpox_fc <- map_dfr(snapshots, run_snapshot)
```

The figure shows both models fitted to the nowcast input, against the
counts as reported (crosses) and after adjustment (dots).

```{r plot-mpox-forecast, fig.height = 7}
plot_df <- mpox_fc |> filter(input_type == "Nowcast")
truth_weeks <- mpox_fc |> distinct(snapshot, week_end, truth, step)
input_pts <- mpox_fc |>
  filter(
    model == "GMITS", step <= 0,
    input_type %in% c("Reported", "Nowcast")
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    data = truth_weeks,
    aes(week_end, truth, alpha = step > 0),
    fill = "grey60", width = 5
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = plot_df |> filter(step >= 0, !is.na(lower)),
    aes(week_end, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill = model_cols[["GMITS"]], alpha = 0.18
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = plot_df,
    aes(week_end, point, color = model),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = input_pts,
    aes(week_end, input, shape = input_type),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = distinct(mpox_fc, snapshot),
    aes(xintercept = snapshot + 0.5),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ snapshot, labeller = label_both, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Reported" = 4, "Nowcast" = 16),
    labels = c("Reported" = "reported at T", "Nowcast" = "nowcast"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = 0.45, "TRUE" = 0.85),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "fit window (final)", "TRUE" = "forecast (final)"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, NA)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical") +
  labs(
    title = "England mpox — 2-week forecasts from nowcast-adjusted input",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Bars = final counts; crosses = reported at T; ",
      "dots = nowcast-adjusted\n",
      "Ribbon = GMITS 95% bootstrap PI (clipped at 0)"
    ),
    x = "Week ending (day index)", y = "Weekly cases"
  )
```

---

# Sliding Window: Error by Input

Within the sliding window, the question that matters in real time is
how each model performs on the data actually available on day *T*. The figure shows the one-week-ahead
absolute percentage error at every snapshot for each input; the bar marks
the mean over snapshots.

```{r plot-truncation, fig.height = 4.2}
ape_df <- mpox_fc |>
  filter(step == 1) |>
  mutate(ape = 100 * abs(point - truth) / truth)

ape_mean <- ape_df |>
  group_by(input_type, model) |>
  summarise(ape = mean(ape), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(ape_df, aes(input_type, ape, color = model)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitterdodge(
      jitter.width = 0.12, dodge.width = 0.6, seed = 1
    ),
    size = 2, alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_crossbar(
    data = ape_mean,
    aes(ymin = ape, ymax = ape),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.6),
    width = 0.5, linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 3.55, y = Inf, label = "not available\nin real time",
    hjust = 0, vjust = 1.2, size = 3, color = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    title = "One-week-ahead error by input and model (6 snapshots)",
    subtitle = "Points = snapshots; bar = mean absolute percentage error",
    x = NULL, y = "APE (%)"
  )
```

```{r error-summary}
mpox_fc |>
  filter(step > 0) |>
  mutate(
    ape = 100 * abs(point - truth) / truth,
    covered = truth >= lower & truth <= upper
  ) |>
  group_by(input_type, model, step) |>
  summarise(
    MAE = mean(abs(point - truth)),
    MAPE = mean(ape),
    bias = median(point - truth),
    coverage = 100 * mean(covered),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(step, input_type, model) |>
  mutate(step = paste(step, if_else(step == 1, "week", "weeks"))) |>
  select(step, input_type, model, MAE, MAPE, bias, coverage) |>
  kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c(
      "Horizon", "Input", "Model", "MAE", "MAPE (%)",
      "Median error", "GMITS 95% PI coverage (%)"
    ),
    caption = "England mpox: out-of-sample error over 6 snapshots (n = 5)"
  ) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, valign = "top")
```

Four points stand out.

- **On the data available in real time, the ranking depends on how
  truncation is handled.** On the raw or ×1.5 input the exponential
  regression is more accurate one week ahead. On the nowcast input the
  two are similar one week ahead (MAPE 27.8% vs. 30.3%) and GMITS is
  clearly better two weeks ahead (28.0% vs. 82.1%).
- **GMITS improves steadily as the input becomes more complete**
  (one-week MAPE 59% → 46% → 28% → 17% from reported to oracle). The
  regression does not: it is least accurate on the complete oracle input
  (91%). Its log-linear slope is dominated by the small counts at the
  start of the window and overshoots (snapshots 75–85 in the figure
  above); on truncated input the depressed final week flattens the slope
  and partly cancels that overshoot. Its advantage on the raw reported
  data is therefore two errors offsetting each other rather than
  robustness to truncation.
- **The simple nowcast closes about three quarters of the gap** in
  GMITS's one-week error between reported and oracle input. The
  remaining shortfall comes mainly from the last two to three days, which
  a point correction cannot recover.
- **The bootstrap intervals remain poorly calibrated** with five weekly
  points (coverage 33–83% against a nominal 95%), so they should not be
  read as calibrated until the planned simulation study has quantified
  their coverage.

Six snapshots from one outbreak are not enough to rank the two methods in
general; the comparison is meant to show which errors dominate.

## Revision history {#revision-history}

Only changes that affect reported results or their interpretation are listed.

| Date | Change | Effect on results |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2026-05-23 | Initial analysis | — |
| 2026-10-13 | Corrected the `gmits()` regression. Integrating $dx^{(1)}/dt + a x^{(1)} = b$ over each interval gives $x^{(0)}_{k} = -a z_{k} + b$; the previous code regressed on $(-z_{k}\Delta t_{k}, \Delta t_{k})$, which shrank $(\hat a, \hat b)$ by $1/\Delta t$ whenever reporting intervals were not one day (and could flip the sign of $\hat a$ on irregular grids). All GMITS pages now load one shared function file. | Synthetic growth scenario: $\hat a$ −0.116 → −0.357 (true −0.4). Listeria (n = 6) MAPE 90.25% → 45.45% (exp. regression 50.20%). Bongkrek (n = 4) MAPE 81.19% → 58.05% (exp. regression 64.47%). With 4 and 1 verifiable steps, these do not establish that either method is more accurate. |
| 2026-10-14 | Replaced the real-data evaluation with real-time snapshots of the 2022 England mpox outbreak (person-to-person transmission; reporting-triangle snapshots at six growth-phase forecast origins, weekly counts, n = 5). The right-truncation section now compares reported, ×1.5-adjusted and backfilled (oracle) inputs instead of fixed scaling factors. The Bongkrek and Listeria analyses remain on their own pages as common-source examples. | New headline results (1 week ahead, 6 snapshots): GMITS MAPE 59.2% on reported input, 17.2% on oracle input; exponential regression 35.6%. 95% PI coverage 33% (reported) and 67% (oracle). Only 21–47% of the most recent week had been reported at each snapshot. |
| 2026-10-14 | Added a delay-based nowcast of the truncated input (stage 1: point correction using the authors' real-time Weibull reporting-delay estimates; days with less than 50% expected reporting imputed from the rest of the week) and fitted the exponential regression to every input, not only the reported one. | One week ahead, MAPE GMITS vs. exponential regression: reported 59.2% vs. 35.6%, nowcast 27.8% vs. 30.3%, oracle 17.2% vs. 91.4%. Two weeks ahead on nowcast input: 28.0% vs. 82.1%. The nowcast raises the reported share of the latest week from 21–47% to 45–91%. |
| 2026-10-14 | Corrected the explanation of the background-value bias. The earlier text said the endpoint mean *understates* the interval mean of a convex $x^{(1)}$ and that the bias runs in the opposite direction and is smaller in the decay phase. In fact the endpoint mean overstates it for a convex curve, and in both phases the bias attenuates $\lvert\hat a\rvert$ by the same factor for a given $\lvert a\rvert\,\Delta t$; only the sign of the forecast error differs. The decay scenario's better fit comes from its smaller $\lvert a\rvert$ and the irregular grid. | No numbers changed. |
| 2026-10-14 | Redesigned the synthetic validation as a 2 × 2 design: growth and decay, each at $\lvert a\rvert$ = 0.3 and 0.4, with $b$, the first value and the time grid held fixed, plus an equally spaced grid and the theoretical attenuation for comparison. The previous two scenarios differed in $\lvert a\rvert$, $b$ and the first value, so they could not separate direction from speed. | Irregular grid, $\hat a / a$: growth 0.933 and 0.892, decay 0.978 and 0.957 (for $\lvert a\rvert$ = 0.3 and 0.4). Equal grid: 0.956 and 0.924 in both directions, equal to theory. |
| 2026-10-14 | Added the core evaluation: forecasts from the first n weekly reports of the outbreak (n = 4–8, forecast origins T = 75–103, each using that day's snapshot), for GMITS and the exponential regression on reported, nowcast and oracle input. The sliding-window analysis is kept as a complement. | One week ahead on nowcast input, GMITS vs. exponential regression: n = 4: 61% vs. 50%; n = 5: 33% vs. 85%; n = 6: 22% vs. 90%; n = 7: 11% vs. 107%; n = 8 (near the peak): 22% vs. 181%. |
